## Introduction

The aim of this notebook is to use MaxEnt to estimate how climate change will impact the habitat of *Eucalyptus pauciflora subsp. niphophila* for use in an ECBA submission.

The specific criteria being addressed is:

> *2b) **Continuing decline** observed, estimated, inferred or **projected** in any of: (i) extent of occurrence; (ii) area of occupancy; **(iii) area, extent and/or quality of habitat;** (iv) number of locations or subpopulations; (v) number of mature individuals."*

That is, we're trying to quantify the decline in the area of *niphophila* habitat under future climate change projections.

### Some similar analyses

- Ren, Jun, Suhang Li, Yawen Zhang, Qiong Yang, Jiaojiao Liu, Jing Fan, and Yangzhou Xiang. 2025. ‘MaxEnt-Based Evaluation of Climate Change Effects on the Habitat Suitability of Magnolia Officinalis in China’. *Frontiers in Plant Science* 16:1601585. doi:[10.3389/fpls.2025.1601585](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2025.1601585).

### Useful references for MaxEnt modeling:

- Merow, C., Smith, M. J., & Silander, J. A. (2013). A practical guide to MaxEnt for modeling species’ distributions: What it does, and why inputs and settings matter. Ecography, 36(10), 1058–1069. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1600-0587.2013.07872.x
- Elith, J., Phillips, S. J., Hastie, T., Dudík, M., Chee, Y. E., & Yates, C. J. (2011). A statistical explanation of MaxEnt for ecologists: Statistical explanation of MaxEnt. Diversity and Distributions, 17(1), 43–57. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-4642.2010.00725.x

## Data preparation

### Download the occurrence data

The first thing I'll do is import the *E. niphophila* observational data. I'm using the `galah` package, which accesses data compiled by the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA).

This download comes with a bunch of data quality checks which we can use to exclude low quality observations from the training data.

Descriptions of the environmental variables: <https://biocache.ala.org.au/fields?filter=name%3Ael%5B0-9%5D*&max=100&order=DESC&sort=classs>

Descriptions of the data quality variables: <https://github.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-dataquality/wiki>

```{r}
# If niph_raw has already been downloaded, import it. Otherwise, download observations from
# the Atlas of Living Australia, including many metadata columns.

niph_raw_path <- here::here("data/galah/niph_raw.rds")

if (file.exists(niph_raw_path)) {
  niph_raw <- readr::read_rds(niph_raw_path)
} else {
  
  # Construct an API call to galah
  
  niph_raw_call <- galah_call() |>
    identify("Eucalyptus pauciflora subsp. niphophila") |>
    select(
      group = c(
        "basic", # record_id, lat/lon, etc.
        "event", # columns describing the observation process
        "assertions" # data quality checks
      ),
      starts_with("el"), # environmental variables
      "coordinateUncertaintyInMeters",
      "spatiallyValid",
      "isDuplicateOf",
      "outlierLayerCount",
      "year",
      "country",
      "stateProvince",
      "identifiedBy",
      "locality",
      "institutionCode"
    )
  
  # Download our occurrence data
  
  niph_raw <- atlas_occurrences(niph_raw_call)
  
  # Save the raw data as an rds file
  
  write_rds(niph_raw, niph_raw_path)
}

nrow(niph_raw)
```

### Filter out low-quality data

Not all of this data is super high quality, so we can apply some data quality filters to try and filter out unreliable records.

The most important data quality filters are

- [`spatiallyValid`](https://github.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-dataquality/wiki/spatiallyValid)`== TRUE`: Built-in checks to make sure the coordinates are logically consistent

- `is.na(isDuplicateOf)`: The record hasn't been flagged as a duplicate

- [`outlierLayerCount`](https://github.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-dataquality/wiki/outlierLayerCount)`== 0`: The record isn't an outlier when compared with other environmental data.

- [`coordinateUncertaintyInMeters`](https://github.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-dataquality/wiki/coordinate_uncertainty)`<= 1000`: Estimated coordinate uncertainty is less than 1 km. Records with no uncertainty estimate are removed as well.

- I'm also removing records from before 1970, or which aren't in NSW, ACT, or Victoria.

```{r}
niph_raw_filtered <- niph_raw |> 
  filter(
    occurrenceStatus == "PRESENT", # Not actually necissary, but reassuring
    !is.na(decimalLongitude), 
    !is.na(decimalLatitude),
    coordinateUncertaintyInMeters <= 1000,
    spatiallyValid == TRUE,
    is.na(isDuplicateOf),
    outlierLayerCount == 0,
    year >= 1970,
    country == "Australia",
    stateProvince %in% c("Victoria", "Australian Capital Territory", "New South Wales")
  )

# Select a useful subset of columns to use in the rest of the analysis

niph_filtered <- niph_raw_filtered |>
  select(
    "recordID",
    "scientificName",
    "decimalLongitude",
    "decimalLatitude",
    "coordinateUncertaintyInMeters",
    "eventDate",
    "year",
    "basisOfRecord",
    "identifiedBy",
    "locality",
    "stateProvince",
    "dataResourceName",
    "institutionCode"
  )

# Convert the observations into a spatial object

niph_filtered_sf <- st_as_sf(
  niph_filtered, 
  coords = c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"), 
  crs = 4326
)

mapview(niph_raw_filtered_sf)
```

### Targeted outlier removal

Some observations are still suspicious, despite passing the data quality checks. I'll remove these records explicitly.

+--------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| **recordID**                         | **Reason for removal**                                                                  |
+======================================+=========================================================================================+
| 2c4dd780-74ef-4337-893b-250e47aa64a8 | In Grampians NP, well outside known range                                               |
+--------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| f1047be9-66f7-4ba6-9157-d0f1d906fa12 | In Baw Baw NP and from 1994, so likely to be the Baw Baw subspecies (described in 1994) |
|                                      |                                                                                         |
| 56c4cb9d-db98-4f0c-8080-d75a281a5b06 |                                                                                         |
+--------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

```{r}
suspicious_records <- c(
  "2c4dd780-74ef-4337-893b-250e47aa64a8",
  "f1047be9-66f7-4ba6-9157-d0f1d906fa12",
  "56c4cb9d-db98-4f0c-8080-d75a281a5b06"
)

niph_notsus_sf <- niph_filtered_sf |> 
  filter(
    recordID %notin% suspicious_records
  )

mapview(filter(niph_filtered_sf, recordID %in% suspicious_records))
```

### Check the elevations

*Niphophila* is known to inhabit altitudes above 1600 m. To allow for some natural variation we'll allow records down to 1400 m, but any records below this altitude will be removed.

```{r}
# Download a 5 degree tile of 3s elevation data which covers the observations.
# 3s data is on a grid of around 90 m x 90 m, which is more accurate than most of our data.
# The crs is EPSG:4326

elev_3s <- geodata::elevation_3s(lon = 147.5, lat = -37.5, path = here::here("data"))

# Convert our observations to SpatVector for terra

niph_vect <- vect(niph_notsus_sf)

# Extract the elevation at each point

niph_elevs <- extract(elev_3s, niph_vect)

# Construct a buffer around each observation to account for positional uncertainty

niph_buffers <- buffer(
  niph_vect, 
  width = niph_notsus_sf$coordinateUncertaintyInMeters
)

# Extract the maximum and minimum elevations in each buffer zone

niph_elev_ranges <- extract(elev_3s, niph_buffers, fun = range, na.rm = TRUE)

# Join the extracted elevation data back to our raw data set

niph_elev_sf <- niph_notsus_sf |>
  mutate(
    elevation_m = niph_elevs[[2]],
    elevation_m_min = niph_elev_ranges[, 2],
    elevation_m_max = niph_elev_ranges[, 3]
  )

# Filter out records below 1400 m

niph_elev_filter_sf <- niph_elev_sf |> 
  filter(elevation_m >= 1400)

# Have a look at observations at an eleveation below 1400 m

niph_elev_sf |> 
  mutate(below_alt = elevation_m < 1400) |> 
  mapview(zcol = "below_alt")
```

### Australian Alps bioregion

The Australian Alps bioregion will be key in defining our study area. I'll also use it to exclude any final records which might not be where we expect to find *Niphophila*.

```{r}
# The bioregions geodatabase doesn't download automatically. If needed, download it from
# https://fed.dcceew.gov.au/datasets/interim-biogeographic-regionalisation-for-australia-ibra-version-7-1-regions/about

# Import the Australian Alps bioregion polygon

aus_alps <- st_read(here::here("data/IBRA7_regions.gdb")) |>
  filter(REG_NAME_7 == "Australian Alps") |> 
  st_transform(4326) |> 
  st_union()

# Identify any observations outside the bioregion

niph_outside_aus_alps <- niph_elev_filter_sf |> 
  st_filter(aus_alps, .predicate = st_disjoint)

# Plot just the points outside the bioregion

mapview(aus_alps, alpha.regions = 0.5, lwd = 2, alpha = 1) +
  mapview(niph_outside_aus_alps, col.regions = "red")
```

There are three observations outside the bioregion. They're all clustered around Thredbo and only a few hundred metres outside the region. As they're so close to the bioregion I'm inclined to keep them in the data set - the positional uncertainty in both the point data and the bioregion definition mean that excluding them would be arbitrary.

This means we now have our final observations data set.

```{r}
niph <- niph_1400_sf

niph
```

## Notes:

- The CDSM filter of records might be a bit aggressive, so there are probably more records we can use. I'm also not really sure what rationale it's using to filter out records.

- Should there be a date cut-off for observations? Some of them are 50+ years old which isn't exactly present conditions.

- I should also look at the location uncertainty for each observation - DONE

- There are some weird horizontal lines of records in NSW. I think they might be transects, but they could also be observations with rounded latitude. it's probably worth checking. And even if they are transects, they may still be skewing the results.

- I'm not sure about filtering out records below 1300m. It removes some clear data quality issues, but it's probably a bit simplistic.

- Data points can also be excluded based on known range - i.e. niphophila unlikely to be on Baw Baw

## Define the study area

We can define a plausible habitat area using a combination of the Australian Alps bioregion and elevation data.

```{r}
# Import IBRA Bioregions Version 7.1, and select the Australian Alps bioregion
# https://fed.dcceew.gov.au/datasets/interim-biogeographic-regionalisation-for-australia-ibra-version-7-1-regions/about
# Note: This data does not download automatically
aus_alps <- st_read(here::here("data/IBRA7_regions.gdb")) |>
  filter(REG_NAME_7 == "Australian Alps") |> 
  st_transform(4326) |> 
  st_union()

# Download 30s elevation data for Australia - tiles match the climate variables
elev_30s <- geodata::elevation_30s(
  country = "AUS",
  path = here::here("data")
)

elev_30s_crop <- crop(elev_30s, vect(aus_alps), mask = TRUE)
elev_mask <- elev_30s_crop >= 1300

study_area <- elev_mask |> 
  as.polygons() |>  # convert TRUE/FALSE raster mask to vector polygons
  st_as_sf() |> 
  filter(AUS_elv_msk == 1) |>  # keep only cells above threshold (check actual layer name)
  st_union() |> 
  st_transform(4326)

# Simplify the study area
# study_area2 <- study_area |> 
#   drop_crumbs(threshold = set_units(2, km^2)) |> 
#   fill_holes(threshold = set_units(2, km^2)) |> 
#   smooth(method = "ksmooth", smoothness = 3)

mapview(study_area, alpha.regions = 0.5, lwd = 2, alpha = 1) +
  mapview(niph_elev, col.regions = "purple")

# This study area is very jagged. Maybe I should just be using the bioregion? Also, there are still some points which sit outside of this region
```

## Spatial thinning

```{r}
# thin() wants plain lon/lat columns, not an sf geometry column
niph_coords <- niph_elev |> 
  st_transform(4326) |> 
  mutate(
    Longitude = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 1],
    Latitude = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 2],
    species = "niphophila" # spec.col is required even for a single species
  ) |> 
  st_drop_geometry()

thinned <- spThin::thin(
  loc.data = niph_coords,
  lat.col = "Latitude",
  long.col = "Longitude",
  spec.col = "species",
  thin.par = 1, # Thinning distance 1 km, should be similar to cell size
  reps = 100,
  locs.thinned.list.return = TRUE,
  write.files = FALSE,
  write.log.file = FALSE
)

# Keep the dataframe with the most retained records
best_rep <- thinned[[which.max(sapply(thinned, nrow))]]

# Re-join back to the full occurrence data to recover all original columns
niph_thinned <- niph_coords |> 
  semi_join(best_rep, by = c("Longitude", "Latitude")) |> 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326)

mapview(niph_thinned)
```

## Download climate data

We can download climate data from [WorldClim](https://www.worldclim.org/) at 30 second resolution (\~1 km² grid cells).

```{r}
# WorldClim climate data is stored as 30x30 degree tiles. 
# We only need one tile to cover the study area
clim_tile <- geodata::worldclim_tile(
  var = "bio",
  res = "0.5", # 0.5 minute resolution
  lon = 135,
  lat = -45,
  path = here::here("data")
)

# Crop the climate data to our study area
clim <- crop(clim_tile, vect(study_area), mask = TRUE)

# Create a key for interpreting the layer names
bioclim_names <- c(
  bio_1  = "Annual Mean Temperature",
  bio_2  = "Mean Diurnal Range",
  bio_3  = "Isothermality",
  bio_4  = "Temperature Seasonality",
  bio_5  = "Max Temperature of Warmest Month",
  bio_6  = "Min Temperature of Coldest Month",
  bio_7  = "Temperature Annual Range",
  bio_8  = "Mean Temperature of Wettest Quarter",
  bio_9  = "Mean Temperature of Driest Quarter",
  bio_10 = "Mean Temperature of Warmest Quarter",
  bio_11 = "Mean Temperature of Coldest Quarter",
  bio_12 = "Annual Precipitation",
  bio_13 = "Precipitation of Wettest Month",
  bio_14 = "Precipitation of Driest Month",
  bio_15 = "Precipitation Seasonality",
  bio_16 = "Precipitation of Wettest Quarter",
  bio_17 = "Precipitation of Driest Quarter",
  bio_18 = "Precipitation of Warmest Quarter",
  bio_19 = "Precipitation of Coldest Quarter"
)

# Plot the first variable - annual mean temperature
mapview(clim$bio_1)
```

## Select predictor variables

Many of these predictor variables are highly co-linear (e.g. Precipitation of Wettest Month and Precipitation of Wettest Quater), and including all of them can cause model instability and make it difficult to assess the importance of each variable.

```{r}
# Generate random background points across the study area
bg_points <- st_sample(study_area, size = 10000, type = "random")

# Extract climate values at these points
clim_vals <- terra::extract(clim, vect(bg_points), ID = FALSE) |> 
  na.omit()

# Calculate a correlation matrix of the variables across our study area
cor_matrix <- cor(clim_vals, method = "pearson")

# For visual inspection of correlations
corrplot::corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "circle", type = "upper")
```

We can use the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) to remove highly correlated predictors.

```{r}
# Remove the four 'interactive' variables which are related to both temperature 
# and precipitation. These variables can have biologically meaningless discontinuities due to
# variation in which quarter counts as wettest or warmest.

interactive_vars <- c("bio_8", "bio_9", "bio_18", "bio_19")

clim_candidates <- clim[[setdiff(names(clim), interactive_vars)]]

# Iteratively remove highly correlated variables using VIF
# th = 10 is a common threshold; th = 5 is stricter
v <- usdm::vifstep(clim_candidates, th = 10, keep = "bio_6") 

clim_selected <- usdm::exclude(clim_candidates, v)

v
```

### Notes

- The decision to use 10,000 background points is totally arbitrary and should probably be justified

- The correlation between two variables being over 0.7 is still quite high

## Fit the current-climate model

We can use `ENMeval` to tune the model's feature classes and regularisation multiplier via spatial cross-validation, rather than picking these settings arbitrarily.

```{r}
# ENMevaluate() wants plain coordinate data frames, not sf objects
occs <- niph_thinned |>
  st_coordinates() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rename(longitude = X, latitude = Y)

bg <- bg_points |>
  st_coordinates() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rename(longitude = X, latitude = Y)

# ENMevaluate() is slow to re-run every time, so cache the result. Delete the
# cache file (or the object below) to force a re-run after upstream changes
# (e.g. to occs, bg, clim_selected, or the tuning settings)
enmeval_results_path <- here::here("data/enmeval_results.rds")

if (file.exists(enmeval_results_path)) {
  enmeval_results <- readr::read_rds(enmeval_results_path)
} else {
  # Tune feature classes (L = linear, Q = quadratic, H = hinge, P = product) and
  # regularisation multiplier, using spatial block partitioning - appropriate
  # here since occurrences are geographically clustered rather than independent
  enmeval_results <- ENMevaluate(
    occs = occs,
    envs = clim_selected,
    bg = bg,
    tune.args = list(fc = c("L", "LQ", "LQH", "LQHP"), rm = seq(0.5, 4, 0.5)),
    partitions = "block",
    algorithm = "maxnet"
  )

  readr::write_rds(enmeval_results, enmeval_results_path)
}

# Inspect tuning results, ranked by AICc (lower = better fit/complexity trade-off)
enmeval_results@results |>
  arrange(AICc)
```

```{r}
# Select the best-supported settings (lowest AICc) and pull out that model
best_settings <- enmeval_results@results |>
  filter(delta.AICc == 0)

maxent_model <- eval.models(enmeval_results)[[best_settings$tune.args]]

# Project habitat suitability across the study area on the cloglog
# (0-1, probability-like) scale
suitability <- terra::predict(clim_selected, maxent_model, type = "cloglog", na.rm = TRUE)

mapview(suitability) +
  mapview(niph_thinned, col.regions = "purple", cex = 3)
```

### Notes

- Feature class/regularisation multiplier combinations are chosen by lowest AICc - worth sanity-checking against cross-validated AUC and omission rate too, both in `enmeval_results@results`

- Block partitioning splits occurrences into 4 spatial folds by default - given how clustered/narrow-ranged this species is, worth checking the fold sizes are reasonable (`enmeval_results@occs.grp`)

## Evaluate the model

```{r}
# Cross-validated performance of the selected feature class / regularisation
# multiplier, from the spatial block cross-validation done during tuning
best_settings |>
  select(fc, rm, auc.val.avg, auc.val.sd, or.10p.avg, or.mtp.avg, AICc)
```

To use this model for quantifying habitat area, we need to convert the continuous suitability surface into a binary suitable/unsuitable classification. We'll use the threshold that maximises the sum of sensitivity and specificity (maxSSS) across the training presence and background points, which tends to be a more robust choice than a fixed percentile threshold (Liu et al. 2013).

```{r}
# Predicted suitability at presence and background locations
# (na.omit drops any points falling on NA cells at the study area's edge)
pred_occs_raw <- terra::extract(suitability, vect(niph_thinned), ID = FALSE)[[1]]
pred_bg_raw <- terra::extract(suitability, vect(bg_points), ID = FALSE)[[1]]

pred_occs <- na.omit(pred_occs_raw)
pred_bg <- na.omit(pred_bg_raw)

# Flag how many points fell outside the study area mask (see earlier note on
# occurrences sitting outside the study area)
message(sum(is.na(pred_occs_raw)), " of ", length(pred_occs_raw), " presence points dropped (NA cell)")
message(sum(is.na(pred_bg_raw)), " of ", length(pred_bg_raw), " background points dropped (NA cell)")

# Find the threshold maximising sensitivity + specificity
candidate_thresholds <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.001)
tss <- sapply(candidate_thresholds, function(t) {
  sensitivity <- mean(pred_occs >= t)
  specificity <- mean(pred_bg < t)
  sensitivity + specificity - 1
})

suitability_threshold <- candidate_thresholds[which.max(tss)]
suitability_threshold
```

```{r}
# Binary suitable/unsuitable habitat map at that threshold
suitable_habitat <- suitability >= suitability_threshold

mapview(suitable_habitat) +
  mapview(niph_thinned, col.regions = "purple", cex = 3)
```

### Notes

- `or.10p.avg`/`or.mtp.avg` are cross-validated omission rates (10th percentile and minimum training presence) - worth checking these are reasonably low for the selected settings, not just the AICc ranking

- `suitability_threshold` will be reused later to quantify suitable habitat area under current and future climate

## Download future climate projections

We can download future climate projections from WorldClim's CMIP6 downscaled data. As with the current-climate data, we use `cmip6_tile()` rather than `cmip6_world()` so we only download the one 30x30 degree tile covering our study area, rather than a global raster (`cmip6_world()` has no `lon`/`lat` argument - it always fetches the full-extent global GeoTIFF, \~1-6+ GB per GCM/SSP/time combination, which isn't practical here).

Rather than a single climate model, we use a spread of GCMs (Global Climate Models) so we can later assess how much projected habitat change depends on the choice of model. We also use all four SSPs (emissions scenarios) available in WorldClim's CMIP6 data, and three time periods spanning short- to long-term projections.

```{r}
# GCMs chosen to span a range of climate sensitivity (cooler to hotter projections)
future_gcms <- c("MIROC6", "MPI-ESM1-2-HR", "IPSL-CM6A-LR", "ACCESS-CM2")

# All four SSPs (emissions scenarios) available from WorldClim's CMIP6 data:
# SSP1-2.6 (low), SSP2-4.5 (moderate), SSP3-7.0 (high), SSP5-8.5 (very high)
future_ssps <- c("126", "245", "370", "585")

# Near-, mid-, and long-term projections
future_time <- c("2021-2040", "2041-2060", "2061-2080")

future_scenarios <- expand.grid(
  gcm = future_gcms,
  ssp = future_ssps,
  time = future_time,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Download each GCM/SSP/time tile (same tile as the current-climate download
# above), crop to the study area, and subset to the same VIF-selected predictors
future_clim <- pmap(future_scenarios, function(gcm, ssp, time) {
  clim_future_tile <- geodata::cmip6_tile(
    lon = 135,
    lat = -45,
    model = gcm,
    ssp = ssp,
    time = time,
    var = "bio",
    path = here::here("data")
  )

  # cmip6_tile() returns the same 19 bioclim variables, in the same order,
  # as worldclim_tile() above - reuse those names so we can subset by the
  # VIF-selected predictor names
  names(clim_future_tile) <- names(clim)

  crop(clim_future_tile, vect(study_area), mask = TRUE)[[names(clim_selected)]]
})

names(future_clim) <- paste(future_scenarios$gcm, future_scenarios$ssp, future_scenarios$time, sep = "_")

# Spot-check one scenario
mapview(future_clim[[1]]$bio_3)
```

### Notes

- This downloads 48 tiles (4 GCMs x 4 SSPs x 3 time periods) at the same resolution/extent as the current-climate tile, rather than 48 global rasters. Each tile is \~80 MB, so expect \~3.8 GB total (some of this may already be cached from earlier runs)

- Worth double-checking that `names(clim_future_tile) <- names(clim)` is a safe assumption - it relies on both tiles containing the same 19 bioclim variables in the same order, which should hold but hasn't been explicitly verified

- The two \~6 GB `cmip6_world()` files downloaded earlier aren't used by this version of the code and can be deleted if you want to reclaim the disk space

## Project the model onto future scenarios

```{r}
# Project the fitted model onto each future climate scenario, on the same
# cloglog scale as the current-climate prediction, then apply the same
# suitability threshold to get binary suitable/unsuitable habitat
future_suitability <- map(future_clim, \(scenario_clim) {
  terra::predict(scenario_clim, maxent_model, type = "cloglog", na.rm = TRUE)
})

future_suitable_habitat <- map(future_suitability, \(s) s >= suitability_threshold)

# Spot-check one scenario against the current-climate prediction
mapview(suitability, layer.name = "current") +
  mapview(future_suitability[[1]], layer.name = names(future_suitability)[1])
```

### Notes

- `future_suitability` holds the continuous cloglog surface per scenario, and `future_suitable_habitat` the binary version at `suitability_threshold` - both keyed by the same `GCM_SSP_time` names as `future_clim`

- This applies the *current* suitability threshold to future predictions, which is standard practice, but worth being explicit about in the write-up

## Quantify habitat change over time

```{r}
# Area (km^2) of suitable habitat in a binary TRUE/FALSE raster
suitable_area_km2 <- function(habitat_raster) {
  areas <- expanse(habitat_raster, unit = "km", byValue = TRUE)
  suitable <- areas$area[areas$value == 1]
  if (length(suitable) == 0) 0 else suitable
}

current_area_km2 <- suitable_area_km2(suitable_habitat)

# future_scenarios and future_suitable_habitat share the same row order, since
# both were built from the same pmap() call earlier
ssp_labels <- c(
  "126" = "SSP1-2.6", "245" = "SSP2-4.5", "370" = "SSP3-7.0", "585" = "SSP5-8.5"
)

habitat_change <- future_scenarios |>
  mutate(
    area_km2 = map_dbl(future_suitable_habitat, suitable_area_km2),
    current_area_km2 = current_area_km2,
    change_km2 = area_km2 - current_area_km2,
    pct_change = 100 * change_km2 / current_area_km2,
    # Ordered factor so the time periods plot in chronological order
    time = factor(time, levels = c("2021-2040", "2041-2060", "2061-2080"), ordered = TRUE),
    ssp_label = factor(ssp_labels[ssp], levels = ssp_labels)
  )

habitat_change
```

```{r}
ggplot(habitat_change, aes(x = time, y = pct_change, colour = gcm, group = gcm)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ssp_label) +
  labs(
    title = "Projected change in suitable habitat area over time",
    x = "Time period", y = "Change in suitable area (%)", colour = "GCM"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

### Notes

- `suitable_area_km2()` sums the area of TRUE cells via `terra::expanse()`, which accounts for cell area distortion (relevant since we're in unprojected lon/lat)

- Worth also reporting the *current* suitable area (`current_area_km2`) as its own figure/stat, not just the % change, since that's part of criterion 2b(iii) too

- Each point is still a single time-slice projection, not a continuous trajectory - worth being explicit about that in the write-up rather than implying a smooth trend between the three time periods

- This only compares suitable habitat *area* - a spatial comparison (e.g. where habitat is lost vs. gained, or a centroid shift) would strengthen the "extent" and "quality" parts of the criterion, and might be worth adding
